findings.title: Rotated PDF pages render blank figures: image bboxes are in unrotated space, the pixmap clip is in rotated space
findings.detail: _image_regions (L121-127) takes page.get_image_info() bboxes (unrotated page coordinates) and intersects them with page.rect (rotated coordinates). _render (L200-214) then passes that rect as clip= to page.get_pixmap(), which expects rotated coordinates. get_text('words') (L206) is also unrotated. I reproduced this: a 612x792 page with set_rotation(90) and one image at (50,100,250,250) gives figure P1.1 with mean pixel 255.0 and 100% white. The picture is lost, and every image check silently analyses an empty white rectangle. Landscape (/Rotate 90) pages are common in supplementary PDFs that hold wide figures and blots.
findings.failure_scenario: A supplementary PDF has a landscape page with /Rotate 90 holding a western-blot montage. The figure is rendered as a blank white crop, segment() finds no panels, and duplicate, clone and splice checks never see the blot. The report still says the file was 'analysed'.
findings.fix: Normalise every coordinate into the rotated (display) space as soon as it is read: r = pymupdf.Rect(info['bbox']) * page.rotation_matrix in _image_regions, _native_dpi and the image_boxes loop of _render, and do the same for word rects (pymupdf.Rect(w[:4]) * page.rotation_matrix) and for caption blocks in _captions. I checked that clip = bbox * page.rotation_matrix renders the image (mean 93.9 instead of 255). Add a regression test with a rotated page.

verdict.reason: Confirmed by reproduction (PyMuPDF 2.0, project venv). pdfdoc.py has no rotation handling anywhere. _image_regions (L121-127) takes get_image_info() bboxes, which are in unrotated page space, and intersects them with page.rect, which is in rotated space. _render (L200-202) then passes that rect as clip= to get_pixmap, which expects rotated (display) coordinates. Test: a 612x792 page with an image at (50,100,250,250) and set_rotation(90), run through pdfdoc.load(). It gives figure P1.1 with shape (313,417), mean 255.0 and 100% white pixels. Clipping with Rect(bbox)*page.rotation_matrix = (542,50,692,250) renders the image (mean about 127). The bug can also lose an image entirely: when the unrotated bbox lies outside the rotated page.rect (for example y>612 on a portrait page rotated to 792x612), the & page.rect intersection crops or drops the region. /Rotate 90 landscape pages are realistic in supplementary PDFs. One part of the reviewer's analysis is wrong, and it affects the proposed fix: get_text('words'/'blocks') returns coordinates in UNROTATED space, and its clip= argument is also read in unrotated space. I verified that get_text('words', clip=unrotated_rect) finds the words, while clip=unrotated_rect*rotation_matrix returns []. So converting every coordinate to rotated space straight after reading it (including _captions and the word clip) would break text extraction at L206. Keeping caption/region matching in unrotated space is consistent, because image bboxes and text blocks share that space.
verdict.corrected_fix: Keep all region/caption geometry in unrotated space (_image_regions, _assign_captions, _captions and _native_dpi are internally consistent and need no change, except the `& page.rect` in _image_regions, which should become `& page.cropbox`/`page.mediabox`-derived unrotated bounds, e.g. `page.rect * page.derotation_matrix`). Convert only at render time in _render: `M = page.rotation_matrix; rclip = clip * M; pix = page.get_pixmap(clip=rclip, ...); k = pix.width / rclip.width; words = page.get_text('words', clip=clip)` (unrotated clip, as now). Then map each word rect with `wr = pymupdf.Rect(w[:4]) * M`, and each image box with `r = (pymupdf.Rect(info['bbox']) & clip) * M`, before offsetting by rclip.x0/rclip.y0 and scaling by k. Set page_box from rclip so the web/Mac overlays (which draw on the rendered page) line up. Add a regression test: a page with an inserted image and set_rotation(90), asserting that the figure is not blank and that its text_boxes/image_boxes fall inside the image.

findings.title: JATS figure ids collide: 'Extended Data Fig. 1', 'Figure 1-figure supplement 1' and file-stem labels all become the same id
findings.detail: _fig_id() takes the first (S?\d+) in the label. I confirmed that 'Figure 1', 'Extended Data Fig. 1', 'Figure 1—figure supplement 1' and 'Appendix 1—figure 2' all map to F1. When the JATS label is missing, fetch.py L376 falls back to the file stem, so 'pone.0123456.g001' and 'pone.0123456.g002' both become F0123456. Nothing makes the ids unique (pdfdoc._name_figures does, sources.load L108-113 does not). Effects: (1) pipeline._analyse L357 writes figures/<id>.png, so later figures overwrite earlier ones; (2) panel ids repeat (F1.a twice), so Feat keys, the dedup key in imgdup.find L273-277 and evidence stems dup-<a>-<b> collide and overwrite; (3) server._panel crops panels out of the overwritten PNG and returns the first id match, so the apps show the wrong pixels; (4) _match_finding treats Figure 1 and Extended Data Fig. 1 panels as the same figure.
findings.failure_scenario: A Nature paper fetched from PMC has Figure 1 and Extended Data Fig. 1. Both get id F1. figures/F1.png ends up holding the Extended Data image, the panel boxes of main Figure 1 are drawn on it in the UI, and the evidence files for two different duplicate pairs overwrite each other.
findings.fix: Build the id from the full label: map 'Extended Data Fig. N' to EDN, '<fig> N—figure supplement M' to FN-SM and 'Appendix N—figure M' to AN-FM. Do not take digits from file stems; use F{k+1} when there is no label. Finally de-duplicate with the same suffix scheme as pdfdoc._name_figures (keep a used-ids dict and append -2, -3 and so on).

verdict.reason:
I confirmed this in the code and by running _fig_id(). In engine/paperinspector/sources.py L134-137, _fig_id builds the id from the first (S?\d+) match in the label. Running it maps 'Figure 1', 'Extended Data Fig. 1', 'Figure 1—figure supplement 1' and 'Appendix 1—figure 2' all to F1. It maps 'pone.0123456.g001' and 'pone.0123456.g002' both to F0123456. The stem fallback comes from fetch.py L376 ("label": label or p.stem).

sources.load L107-113 assigns these ids directly, with no de-duplication step like pdfdoc._name_figures (pdfdoc.py L222-234). It then replaces paper.figures with them.

The collision is easy to hit with real papers. Nature papers on PMC tag Extended Data figures as <fig> elements with labels like 'Extended Data Fig. 1', and eLife tags figure supplements the same way. So the main Figure 1 and its counterparts share the id F1.

Effects I verified:
- pipeline._analyse L357 (and L472) writes figures/{f.id}.png, so the later figure overwrites the earlier one.
- panels.py L60 builds panel ids as f"{fig.id}.{l}", so panel ids such as F1.a repeat.
- server._panel L165-172 returns the first panel whose id matches, then crops it out of figures/{fig id}.png. That file holds whichever figure was written last, so the apps show the wrong pixels.

I did not trace the knock-on effects on the imgdup dedup key or the evidence filenames line by line. They follow from the repeated panel ids. The overwrite and wrong-crop failures alone are enough to confirm the bug.
verdict.corrected_fix:
In sources.py, replace _fig_id with a parser that reads the whole label:
- 'Extended Data Fig(ure). N' -> EDN
- '<Fig|Figure> N—figure supplement M' (em dash, en dash or hyphen) -> FN-SM
- 'Appendix N—figure M' -> AN-FM
- 'Supplementary Fig(ure). N' / 'Fig. SN' -> FSN
- a plain 'Fig(ure) N' -> FN

Fall back to F{k+1} when the label has no recognisable figure number. Never take digits from a file stem: in fetch.py L376, pass label=label (possibly empty) and keep p.stem only as the display label. Then, in sources.load L108-113, de-duplicate the ids with a used-ids dict and append -2, -3 and so on, the same way pdfdoc._name_figures does. That keeps figures/<id>.png, the panel ids and the evidence stems unique.

findings.title: Overlapping raster placements (inset on top of a big raster) become two panels with the same pixels and are reported as a duplicate
findings.detail: When a figure has two or more placed rasters, segment() XY-cuts every box covering at least 35% of the figure and adds every smaller box as its own panel (L32-38), even when the small raster lies inside the big one. The rendered figure is a composite, so the inset's pixels are also inside the big raster's panel. I reproduced this: a 400x300 pt raster with a 110x110 pt inset raster on top gives panels F2.a (the whole figure) and F2.b (the inset), and imgdup.find returns a match with ncc_dog 0.97, frac_b 0.95. _match_finding turns that into an integrity finding 'F2.b is a crop of F2.a'. Nothing anywhere suppresses matches between panels whose figure-space boxes overlap.
findings.failure_scenario: A figure is one raster montage, and the publisher or author has placed a magnified inset, scale bar or colour key raster on top. The scan reports 'F3.d is a crop of F3.a' as an image-duplication integrity signal (scored), which is a false accusation.
findings.fix: In segment(), drop any placed box that is at least 80% contained in a larger placed box, or remove the contained region from the parent before XY-cutting. Also, in imgdup.find, or in pipeline before reporting, discard matches where both panels belong to the same figure and their figure-space boxes intersect (IoU > 0 after mapping box_a and box_b by the panel offsets).

verdict.reason:
I confirmed this from the code and by running it. I made no edits; the only file I wrote was a repro script in the scratchpad.

Code path:
- pdfdoc.py:209-213 records every placed raster's bbox in `fig.image_boxes`, including rasters that sit on top of other rasters.
- In panels.py:29-38, when there are two or more placed boxes, any box covering at least 35% of the figure is XY-cut and every smaller box is appended as its own panel. Nothing checks whether one box contains another.
- A big montage raster with an inset drawn on top has no white gutter around the inset, so `_xycut` does not split there. The parent panel (F2.a) is the whole rendered composite, and it contains the inset's pixels.
- The inset also becomes its own panel (F2.b).
- `imgdup.candidates` (imgdup.py:108-153) only skips descriptor matches within the same panel (`o == me`). `verify` and `find` (imgdup.py:266-279) do not filter by figure or by figure-space overlap.
- `pipeline._match_finding` (pipeline.py:43-127) does not check whether the two panels overlap in the figure either. `_image_findings` (pipeline.py:216-221) reports every match.

Repro, run with the project's .venv:
- I built an 800x600 textured micrograph with a 220x220 magnified inset pasted at (560,20), with `image_boxes=[[0,0,800,600],[560,20,220,220]]`.
- segment() returned F2.a = whole figure and F2.b = the inset.
- imgdup.find matched them with ncc_dog 0.91, frac_a 0.095, frac_b 0.947, scale 1.0005. That is the inset matching its own pixels inside F2.a, not the region it magnifies.
- _match_finding produced an "integrity" finding with severity "medium" and the title "F2.b is a crop of F2.a".
- The `crop_of` path (pipeline.py:103-110) only downgrades the severity one step. It still reports the inset as a duplicate even though the two panels share their rendered pixels.

This is a realistic layout: magnified insets, colour keys and logos placed as separate rasters on top of a figure raster are common.
verdict.corrected_fix:
Fix this with two changes. Do not just drop contained boxes: that would stop the inset being checked against other panels.

1. panels.py segment(), after building `placed`: for each small box that is at least 80% inside a big (35% or more) placed box, still emit the small box as its own panel. Also record its rectangle, so that when the big box's leaf panels are built, the inset area is added to that panel's exclusion mask (`text_mask`, or a new `overlay_mask` that imgdup.features honours the way it does `tmask`). Then the parent panel does not carry keypoints from the inset's pixels.

2. As a backstop for any other overlapping-panel case, in pipeline._image_findings (around L216), and also in imgdup.find if preferred, skip a match when `pa.figure_id == pb.figure_id` and the matched regions occupy the same place in the figure. Map each region into figure coordinates: `ra = [pa.box.x + m.box_a[0], pa.box.y + m.box_a[1], m.box_a[2], m.box_a[3]]`, and likewise `rb` from pb. Skip the match when IoU(ra, rb) > 0.5 and abs(m.geo["scale"] - 1) < 0.1 and not m.flip. Use a meaningful IoU threshold rather than "IoU > 0" so that a genuine magnified-inset relation, where the inset magnifies a different region, still surfaces as the existing "may be a magnified view" note.

Add a regression test, for example in tests/: a Figure with `image_boxes` holding a big raster plus a small inset on top, asserting that no image.duplicate finding names the parent panel and its inset as copies of the same pixels.

findings.title: Archive unpacking flattens paths: same-named members overwrite each other and are then analysed twice; ids also collide after 26 members
findings.detail: _unpack writes each member to out / Path(info.filename).name (L205, L215) and appends dest every time. 'Fig1/panelA.tif' and 'Fig2/panelA.tif' both go to out/panelA.tif: the second overwrites the first, and members holds the same path twice. _supplement (L188-189) then loads that one file twice as figures S1a and S1b. They are pixel-identical, so imgdup reports 'S1a.a and S1b.a appear to show the same image' (high, downgraded to medium only because the id starts with 'S'). The first file is never analysed. Separately, the prefix f'{prefix}{chr(97 + k % 26)}' repeats for k >= 26 (members[:30]): member 27 gets 'S1b' like member 2, which brings the figure-PNG and panel-id collisions described for JATS ids.
findings.failure_scenario: A supplementary zip holds per-figure folders that each contain 'blot.tif'. The report flags a scored duplicate between two supplementary images that are really one file analysed twice, and the other blots are never examined.
findings.fix: Keep paths unique: dest = out / f'{i:03d}_{Path(name).name}' (or keep the sanitised relative path inside out, still rejecting '..'), and skip a dest that has already been written. Generate prefixes without wrapping, for example f'{prefix}.{k + 1}' or base-26 with two letters.

verdict.reason: I checked the code and the bug is real. In engine/paperinspector/sources.py, _unpack writes every zip member to `out / Path(info.filename).name` (L205) and every tar member to `out / Path(m.name).name` (L215), so the folder part of each path is dropped. It appends `dest` every time and never checks whether that path was already written. So 'Fig1/blot.tif' and 'Fig2/blot.tif' both end up at out/blot.tif. The second write replaces the first, and `members` lists the same Path twice. At L188-189, _supplement walks `members[:30]` and calls itself once per entry. The IMAGE_EXT branch (L173-180) then reads the one surviving file twice and adds it as two figures, with ids f"{prefix}a" and f"{prefix}b" (for example S1a and S1b). Nothing removes identical images before the comparison: imgdup has only a dhash for chart panels, and pipeline.py uses hashlib for something else (L36). So the two pixel-identical figures are compared, and pipeline.py L86-90 titles the result "... appear to show the same image". Its severity is high, or critical if the transform check fires. Because the ids start with 'S', L98-103 lowers it one step, so a plain copy is reported as medium. Either way it is a scored image.duplicate finding, and the overwritten first blot is never analysed. Per-figure folders that reuse file names (blot.tif, panelA.tif, image1.png) are common in supplementary zips, so realistic input triggers this. The id collision is also real: chr(97 + k % 26) gives k=26 the same letter as k=0, and k=27 the same as k=1. The loop takes up to 30 members, so in an archive with more than 26 files, member 27 gets the same figure id as member 1 (S1a), and the same for 28/2, 29/3 and 30/4. That holds even after the path fix. One small correction to the report: the k=26 collision lands on 'S1a', and 'S1b' collides at k=27.
verdict.corrected_fix: In _unpack, make each output path unique. Either keep the relative path, cleaned and rejecting '..' or absolute paths and joined under `out`, or add the member index: `dest = out / f"{i:03d}_{Path(name).name}"`. Skip or rename any dest already in a `seen` set. In _supplement L189, build sub-prefixes without wrap-around, for example f"{prefix}.{k + 1}" or a two-letter base-26 suffix. Check that the new id format still works with the `"-" in id.split(".")[0]` and `startswith("S")` checks at pipeline.py L98.

findings.title: 16-bit microscope TIFFs are crushed to about 16 grey levels, and transparent PNGs turn black (black labels vanish)
findings.detail: _read_image (and pdfdoc._load_image L34) uses cv2.imread(..., IMREAD_COLOR), which converts 16-bit data by >>8 and drops alpha. I confirmed that a 12-bit-in-16-bit TIFF (0..4095) loads with max value 15, so the image is nearly black and quantised: clone._fine and forensics.flat_patches/dog see no noise (flat_patches returns [] because median noise < 0.8), and SIFT works on a 16-level image. I also confirmed that an RGBA PNG with a transparent background loads with background (0,0,0), so black axis text and labels become black on black (max 0 in the text area). The figure is then segmented on a black ground and OCR and text masking cannot see the labels. The PIL fallback has the same problem: im.convert('RGB') clips 'I;16' and 'I' modes to 255.
findings.failure_scenario: A supplementary raw-image TIFF from a microscope (12-bit in 16-bit) is 'analysed' but every noise-based check is blind, so a pasted rectangle or cloned cells go undetected. A transparent-background PNG figure from Prism or PowerPoint loses all its labels, so text masking fails and repeated glyphs can reach the clone detector.
findings.fix: Read with cv2.IMREAD_UNCHANGED (or PIL), then normalise. For uint16 or float data, stretch the 0.1-99.9 percentiles to 0..255. For 2-D data, use GRAY2BGR. For 4 channels, alpha-composite onto white: rgb*a + 255*(1-a). Put this in one shared helper used by sources._read_image, pdfdoc._load_image and the docx imdecode path.

verdict.reason:
I tried to refute this and couldn't: the bug is real and I reproduced it with the project's own .venv. All three decode paths read images as 8-bit 3-channel: engine/paperinspector/sources.py:56 (`cv2.imread(..., cv2.IMREAD_COLOR)`), pdfdoc.py:34 (same call) and the docx path at sources.py:168 (`cv2.imdecode(..., IMREAD_COLOR)`). The PIL fallback at sources.py:61 calls `im.convert("RGB")`, which clips 16-bit data.

Realistic inputs reach this code. IMAGE_EXT at sources.py:20 includes .tif and .tiff, and `_supplement` (around L174) sends supplementary image files, archive members and JATS figure files (L106) through `_read_image`. An uploaded image goes through `pdfdoc._load_image`. Nothing between decode and analysis rescales the data: the `cv2.normalize` calls in clone.py:60 and imgdup.py:80 stretch an image that is already quantised, so they cannot bring back the lost levels.

What I ran:
- **12-bit data stored in a 16-bit TIFF** (values about N(2000, 200), clipped to 0..4095): `sources._read_image` returned uint8 with min 4, max 11 and only 8 distinct values. That is far below the 0.8 median-noise floor in forensics.py:89, so the noise-based checks see nothing.
- **RGBA PNG** (black opaque box on a background with RGB 0 and alpha 0): `_read_image` and `pdfdoc._load_image` both returned max 0 for the whole image. The black content disappears into the black background.
- **PIL with a 16-bit image:** an 'I;16' image converted to RGB gives max 255, so it saturates.

Two caveats limit the impact but don't refute the bug:
1. A TIFF that really uses the full 16-bit range loses only its low bits when converted.
2. Transparent pixels only turn black when the exporter stored RGB=0 under alpha=0. That is common but not universal.

The fix the reviewer proposed is sound.
verdict.corrected_fix:
Add one shared helper (for example `imageio_util.to_bgr8(arr)`) and use it in sources._read_image, pdfdoc._load_image and the docx imdecode path at sources.py:168. Decode with cv2.IMREAD_UNCHANGED, or use np.array(PIL.Image) when cv2 returns None, and keep the original dtype. Then:

1. If there are 4 channels, alpha-composite onto white in float: rgb*a + 255*(1-a), with a = alpha / max of the alpha dtype. Composite before any intensity stretch.
2. If the data is not uint8 (uint16, int32 or float), stretch the 0.1 to 99.9 percentiles to 0..255. Skip the stretch when hi <= lo, and fall back to the dtype's max in that case.
3. If the image is 2-D (or 2-channel gray plus alpha), convert with GRAY2BGR.
4. Return contiguous uint8 BGR, then apply the existing 2400 px downscale.

For PIL modes 'I;16' and 'I', use np.array(im) directly. Do not call im.convert('RGB'). For multi-page TIFFs, take the first page; cv2.imread already does this.

findings.title: Evidence images for thin blot strips grow to tens of thousands of pixels wide (36k-px PNG, 23k-px 10 MB GIF, about 7 s per match)
findings.detail: _fit scales to a fixed height (300 for side_by_side, 320 for blink_gif) with no cap on width. I measured pair_evidence on a 30x1800 blot match: pair PNG 300x36012, blink GIF 22976x320 at 10.2 MB, 7.4 s for one match. Blots, the most common duplication target, are exactly these wide, short strips. pipeline._image_findings calls pair_evidence for every match without a limit, so a montage-heavy supplement with dozens of blot matches costs minutes and hundreds of MB. The web and Mac apps then have to decode the huge GIFs.
findings.failure_scenario: A paper with 40 re-used loading-control strips takes several extra minutes to scan, produces about 400 MB of evidence, and the blink viewer stalls the browser on the decoded 23k-px frames.
findings.fix: In _fit, take the smaller of height/h and max_width/w (for example max_width=1400) and pad to the target height. In side_by_side, stack vertically when the aspect ratio is above about 3. Optionally limit how many matches get a GIF, and render the rest on demand through the server's compare endpoint.

verdict.reason:
The defect is real, but the reported cost is overstated. In engine/paperinspector/evidence.py:19-22, _fit scales to a fixed height and has no width cap. A 30-px-tall strip is therefore upscaled 10x (INTER_CUBIC) in both dimensions. side_by_side (line 35-46, height 300) and blink_gif (line 73-81, height 320) inherit this. pair_evidence (line 97-106) is called with no cap for every match at pipeline.py:217-220 (and at 479-483 for cross-paper matches).

Thin strips are realistic panels: panels.py:16 sets MIN_PANEL=28, and the 3-px flat-gap splitting at panels.py:123-124 separates stacked blot rows into individual strips.

I reproduced the geometry exactly: for a 30x1800 match, the pair PNG is 36012x300 and the blink GIF is 22976x320. The 10 MB / 21 MB / 7.4 s figures only hold for random-noise input. With a blot-like synthetic strip they drop to:
- 30x1800: about 4 MB PNG plus 1.4 MB GIF, 0.8 s per match
- 40x600: 9012-px-wide PNG plus 5440-px-wide GIF, 1.8 MB, 0.2 s
- 50x400: 4812-px-wide PNG plus 2808-px-wide GIF

So output is grossly oversized and needlessly upsampled. The pair PNG can exceed common browser and canvas dimension limits (about 32k px). But "minutes and about 400 MB" for 40 matches is an exaggeration: realistic totals are tens of MB and well under a minute.

Separately, the box overlays use sa = height/a.shape[0]. That stays consistent only because the same uniform scale is used. Any fix that changes the scale must update _box scaling in side_by_side, clone_evidence (line 110) and region_evidence (line 129) to match.
verdict.corrected_fix: Make _fit compute one scale s = min(height/h, max_width/w, max_upscale) with, for example, max_width=1200 and max_upscale=3, and return the resized image plus s. Callers then use the returned s for _box and line coordinates instead of recomputing height/shape[0]. Afterwards, pad the image to the target height with white (side_by_side, region_evidence) or let frames have their natural size (blink_gif, where fb is already resized to fa.shape). In side_by_side, stack A and B vertically with a horizontal gap when the combined aspect ratio exceeds about 3, so wide blot strips render as two rows. Optionally cap blink-GIF generation to the top N matches by score in pipeline._image_findings and leave the rest to the server's compare endpoint.

findings.title: Supplementary-figure detection by id string misfires: main-paper 'F3-2' is downgraded, JATS 'FS1' is not
findings.detail: _match_finding treats a panel as supplementary when the figure-id part contains '-' or the id starts with 'S'. pdfdoc._name_figures gives a main-paper figure that spans two pages the id 'F3-2' ('Figure 3 (part 2)'), so real within-paper reuse involving it is downgraded one severity step. Meanwhile JATS 'Figure S1' gets id 'FS1' from sources._fig_id and is not recognised as supplementary. The clone severity check (L253, p.figure_id.startswith('S')) has the same blind spot for 'FS1'.
findings.failure_scenario: A duplicated micrograph between Figure 2 and the second page of Figure 3 ('F3-2') is reported as medium instead of high. Montage repeats in supplementary Figure S4 from PMC ('FS4') are reported at full main-paper severity.
findings.fix: Store an explicit Figure.supplementary flag: set it in sources._supplement, in _fig_id when the label has S, 'Supplementary', 'Extended Data' or 'figure supplement', and in pdfdoc when CAPTION_RE matched 'Supplementary' or an S-number. Copy it to Panel and use it in place of the string heuristics.

verdict.reason:
The bug is real; I traced every part of the claim in the code.

1) pdfdoc._name_figures (pdfdoc.py:222-231) gives the second figure that shares a caption number the id f"{base}-{n+1}", for example "F3-2". This happens when a "Figure 3 (continued)" legend on the next page matches CAPTION_RE (pdfdoc.py:18). It also happens when two caption blocks on one page parse to the same number. Panels inherit that id as "F3-2.a" (panels.py:60).

2) pipeline.py:98 computes `supplementary = any("-" in p_.id.split(".")[0] or p_.id.startswith("S") ...)`. For "F3-2.a" the first part is "F3-2", which contains "-", so the panel counts as supplementary. Lines 100-103 then lower an untransformed, within-paper duplicate one step: high becomes medium, critical becomes high. The reported scenario (Figure 2 vs the second part of Figure 3, untransformed) matches this.

3) The id string misses supplementary figures in the other direction. sources._fig_id (sources.py:134-137) turns "Figure S1" into "FS1". pdfdoc builds "F" + number from CAPTION_RE group 2 ("S1"), so a supplementary figure printed in the main or bioRxiv PDF also becomes "FS1". Neither id starts with "S" or contains "-", so both get main-paper severity. The heuristic only works for figures from supplement files, which _supplement renames to "S1-F3" (sources.py:149).

4) The clone check at pipeline.py:253 (`p.figure_id.startswith("S")`) has the same gap for "FS1".

Two caveats:
- The PMC case depends on JATS <fig> elements labelled "Figure S#". Many PMC supplements are <supplementary-material> instead, so it is narrower than the PDF case. The PDF path ("Supplementary Figure S1" captions) is common, though.
- eLife-style "Figure 1—figure supplement 1" labels get "F1" from _fig_id. That also misses the flag and can produce a duplicate id, which strengthens the case for an explicit flag.

The proposed fix (an explicit Figure.supplementary flag copied to Panel) is sound.
verdict.corrected_fix:
Add `supplementary: bool = False` to Figure and Panel, and copy it in panels.py where Panel(...) is built.

Set it in three places:
- In sources._supplement, on every figure taken from a supplement file.
- In sources.load for JATS figures whose label matches `(?i)\bS\d+|supplement|extended data`. Also have _fig_id keep the "figure supplement N" suffix so eLife ids stay unique.
- In pdfdoc._render/_name_figures when CAPTION_RE matched the "Supplementa(l|ry)" prefix or an S-number. This needs a capturing group for the prefix.

Then replace pipeline.py:98 with `supplementary = pa.supplementary or pb.supplementary`, and pipeline.py:253 with `if p.supplementary:`. The "-" check must go, so continuation parts like "F3-2" are no longer downgraded.

findings.title: Single-image uploads bypass the size cap, PIL fallback and format handling that supplements get
findings.detail: scan() on an image goes through pdfdoc._load_image: cv2.imread only, with no 2400-px cap, no PIL fallback and no '.gif' in IMAGE_SUFFIXES (a .gif upload goes to pymupdf.open). sources._read_image does cap at 2400 px and fall back to PIL. A 10000x8000 TIFF upload is processed at full resolution: flat_patches builds full-size float buffers and connected components, the OCR subprocess may hit its 30 s timeout, and the float32 copies take more than 1 GB. An image cv2 cannot decode raises 'cannot read image' with no fallback.
findings.failure_scenario: A user drops in an 80 MP slide scan. The scan takes minutes, uses gigabytes of RAM, and the OCR mask silently times out, so labels are not masked.
findings.fix: Have pdfdoc._load_image call the shared loader (the same normalisation, cap and fallback as sources._read_image), and add .gif to IMAGE_SUFFIXES.

findings.title: MAX_PARTNERS cap uses 'and', so a hub panel gets unlimited candidate verifications
findings.detail: The cap skips a pair only when both panels already have MAX_PARTNERS partners. A panel that shares descriptors with many others (a repeated scale-bar strip, a common background, a periodic texture) keeps collecting partners as long as each partner is still unsaturated, so verify() (BF matching, two RANSAC fits, several warps and periodicity FFTs) runs O(n) times for that hub.
findings.failure_scenario: A supplement with 200 small panels that share a raster scale-bar region makes one hub panel get verified against most of the others, adding tens of seconds to minutes.
findings.fix: Use 'or' (skip when either panel is saturated), or rank partners per panel and keep the top MAX_PARTNERS for each side.

findings.title: Keypoint coordinates are divided by the requested scale, not the actual one, after max(8, int(...)) clamping
findings.detail: _kp resizes to (max(8, int(w*s)), max(8, int(h*s))) but divides the points by s on both axes. For very elongated panels, where int(h*s) < 8 is clamped to 8, the real vertical scale differs from s (for example 8/24 = 0.33 against s = 0.20), so y coordinates come out up to about 65% too large and can fall outside the panel. That distorts the RANSAC geometry, the hull-area test and the text-mask lookup. clone.find (L57, L126) has the same truncation mismatch on a smaller scale.
findings.failure_scenario: Two very long, thin strips that really are copies get an anisotropic fit and are rejected (aniso > 1.35 or a failed warp), or the evidence boxes are drawn in the wrong place.
findings.fix: Compute sx = gs.shape[1] / w and sy = gs.shape[0] / h after resizing and divide x by sx and y by sy. Do the same in clone.find with the real resized dimensions.

findings.title: Photoshop ICC detection is dead code, and multi-page TIFFs are only read on page 1
findings.detail: In _exif, (im.info.get('icc_profile') or b'')[:0] is always empty, so 'Profile: Photoshop' is never set. _read_image uses cv2.imread, which reads only the first page of a multi-page or multi-channel TIFF, yet the file is marked 'analysed' with figures=1.
findings.failure_scenario: A supplementary TIFF stack with 4 channels or fields is reported as analysed, but 3 of its 4 images are never checked for duplication.
findings.fix: Use the whole ICC bytes (for example b'Photoshop' in icc or decoding the profile description) instead of the [:0] slice. Read TIFFs with cv2.imreadmulti, or with PIL ImageSequence for up to N pages, and add each page as its own figure (S3.p1, S3.p2, and so on), or at least set the status to 'analysed (page 1 of N)'.
